findings.title: Tracker SDK: Google Ads (advertising)
findings.why: An identified third-party SDK. Its category decides the WP248 criteria: advertising and attribution build marketing profiles (criterion 1) by combining this app's data with what the vendor collects in other companies' apps (criterion 6); session replay observes the person (criterion 3) and profiles usage (1); anti-fraud scores the person (1) to decide whether they may use a service (9); analytics and push engagement profile usage (1); other categories meet none.

findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: A privacy manifest declares required reason 1C8F.1 for the UserDefaults API: the code reads and writes defaults shared with the apps, extensions and App Clips in the same App Group. Apple permits this only within the group and forbids using it for tracking. Inventory: it shows a shared store exists, not what is stored in it. (The rule id is kept for continuity; it used to fire on any UserDefaults declaration and claimed an advertising-ID share nothing in the bundle showed.)
findings.title: UserDefaults shared within an App Group (declared reason 1C8F.1)
findings.why: Device and environment signals. On their own they meet none of the WP248 criteria; profiling happens in the SDK that combines them, which the tracker rules score.

findings.explanation: PHPhotoLibrary / UIImagePickerController for photo-library access.
findings.title: Photo library (PHPhotoLibrary)
findings.why: The photo library holds personal documents and the location each photo was taken, data of a highly personal nature under WP248 criterion 4. One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard / UIPasteboardChanged, reading the system pasteboard. Background clipboard reads are a well-documented privacy issue.
findings.title: UIPasteboard / generalPasteboard access
findings.why: Access to a store of personal data. The contact list, pasteboard and media library are not among the WP248 high-risk criteria; photos and calendars are scored on their own rules.

findings.explanation: AVCaptureSession / AVCaptureDevice, direct camera capture.
findings.title: Camera capture API
findings.why: Camera and screen capture APIs. Capture alone meets none of the WP248 criteria.

findings.explanation: LSApplicationQueriesSchemes names the scheme of a messenger, social or banking app (tg, vk, whatsapp, telegram, instagram, sberbank, alfabank, vtb, tinkoffbank), so -canOpenURL: can tell whether it is installed.
findings.title: Checks for specific messenger, social or banking apps
findings.why: Which apps are installed says what a person is interested in: WP248 criterion 1 covers profiling from "personal preferences or interests". One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: The app declares URL schemes it can probe with -canOpenURL:, the iOS analogue of Android's QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. A short list (deep-linking into a few partner apps) is routine; a long list is an installed-app fingerprinting signal.
findings.remediation: Trim LSApplicationQueriesSchemes to only the apps you genuinely interoperate with; probing a broad list to fingerprint installed apps risks App Store rejection.
findings.title: Probes installed apps via LSApplicationQueriesSchemes (12 schemes)
findings.why: Which apps are installed says what a person is interested in: WP248 criterion 1 covers profiling from "personal preferences or interests". One criterion is a risk under GDPR, not a likely high risk.

findings.explanation: WKUserScript injects JS at document start/end on every load, useful for telemetry and credential interception.
findings.title: WKUserScript injection
findings.why: The app injects a user script into its WebView.

findings.explanation: WKWebView is the iOS embedded browser.
findings.title: WKWebView in use
findings.why: The app embeds a WebView.

findings.explanation: The app registers custom URL scheme(s) via CFBundleURLSchemes. Any app or web page can invoke these; if application(_:open:options:) acts on unvalidated parameters, this is an entry point for unauthorized actions. Custom schemes are also unverified (unlike Universal Links). Review the handler for input validation.
findings.remediation: Validate and sanitize every parameter in application(_:open:options:); never trigger sensitive actions from a URL without authentication. Prefer Universal Links (verified) over custom schemes.
findings.title: Registers 2 custom URL schemes (inbound deep-link surface)
findings.why: The app registers custom URL schemes. MASWE-0029 makes them a weakness when a sensitive flow relies on them or the handler does not validate input, which MASTG-TEST-0370 and -0371 read from the handler code.

findings.explanation: Legal iOS background-execution channels. `location`/`voip` enable persistent background execution and are the strongest signal; `audio`/`external-accessory` are moderate; `fetch`/`remote-notification`/`processing` are routine and declared by most apps.
findings.remediation: Declare only the background modes the app actually needs; each is reviewed by App Review and must map to genuine user-facing functionality, not background telemetry.
findings.title: Background modes declared: remote-notification
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: content-available=1 silent push lets the server wake the app to refresh data without a visible notification. The `didReceiveRemoteNotification` delegate method appears in almost every push-using app, so it's no longer a primary signal; the silent variant is the `content-available` payload and the `remote-notification` UIBackgroundModes entry together.
findings.title: Content-available silent push
findings.why: Background execution and push modes. None of the WP248 criteria is met by the mode alone.

findings.explanation: Opens a raw socket stream via CFStreamCreatePairWithSocketToHost / NSStream getStreamsToHostWithName. These APIs are not governed by App Transport Security, so TLS is opt-in, a common way cleartext traffic slips past ATS. Confirm the SSL security level is set.
findings.title: Raw CFStream / NSStream socket (bypasses ATS)
findings.why: CFStream and NSStream sockets are not covered by ATS. MASTG-TEST-0323 fails only when such a socket carries cleartext, which depends on whether the code enables TLS on it; that code is FairPlay-encrypted, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: References NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey / isExcludedFromBackup. The key does not guarantee exclusion, and sensitive files still need to be encrypted, so its presence is a reference, not a mitigation.
findings.title: Backup-exclusion API in use (NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey)
findings.why: Records that the app marks files as excluded from backup.

findings.explanation: A binary imports NSFileProtectionNone, the class that leaves a file readable while the device is locked. The import shows the option is referenced, often by a library that maps every protection class; whether it is applied to sensitive data needs the manual review the linked MASTG test describes.
findings.title: References NSFileProtectionNone
findings.why: The import shows the protection class is referenced, not that sensitive data is stored under it.

findings.explanation: Imports rand() / srand() / random() / drand48(), predictable PRNGs unsuitable for tokens, keys, IVs or nonces. Use SecRandomCopyBytes or arc4random_buf. `arc4random() % n` also introduces modulo bias; prefer arc4random_uniform(n).
findings.title: Non-cryptographic random number generator
findings.why: A non-cryptographic generator is linked. MASTG-TEST-0311 fails only when its output is used for keys, tokens or other security values, which is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Imports CC_MD5 / CC_SHA1 (CommonCrypto) or CryptoKit's Insecure.MD5 / Insecure.SHA1. Both are collision-broken and unsuitable for signatures, integrity checks or password hashing, but are also widely used for non-security purposes (cache keys, ETags, file checksums), so the finding is a pointer for review.
findings.title: Weak hash primitive (MD5 / SHA-1)
findings.why: MD5 or SHA-1 is linked. MASTG-TEST-0211 fails only when the hash protects sensitive data; checksums and cache keys pass. That use is in FairPlay-encrypted code, so the scan records the API.

findings.explanation: Binaries carrying 132 debugger (stab) entries in their symbol table: vl_mediasoup_client_ios. Stabs name source files, object files and functions, and often the build machine's paths. They make reverse engineering easier and are not needed to run the app.
findings.remediation: Set Debug Information Format to DWARF with dSYM File for release builds and keep the dSYM out of the app bundle; strip the binaries.
findings.title: Debug symbols left in binaries (1)
findings.why: Leftover debug information eases reverse engineering; MASWE files it under the resilience profile, where it is a finding only when resilience is required.

findings.explanation: A string matching the Google API Key format ships in GoogleService-Info.plist. It identifies the client; it does not authorise access. GoogleService-Info.plist is a Firebase client configuration. A Firebase API key identifies the project; authorisation is enforced server-side by Security Rules, App Check and IAM. An unrestricted key can still be abused against billable Google APIs, and restriction is server-side state the bundle cannot show. Reported for inventory only; it is not a leaked secret.

metrics.reason: GoogleService-Info.plist is a Firebase client configuration. A Firebase API key identifies the project; authorisation is enforced server-side by Security Rules, App Check and IAM. An unrestricted key can still be abused against billable Google APIs, and restriction is server-side state the bundle cannot show.

findings.remediation: No rotation needed. For a Google API key, confirm in the Google Cloud console that it is restricted to this app and to the APIs it uses, and that authorisation is enforced server-side (Firebase Security Rules, App Check).

findings.why: A public client identifier (a Firebase config, an OAuth client id) is meant to ship in the binary. Finding one is not finding a leak.

findings.explanation: The binary imports dlopen/dlsym, so it can resolve and call code chosen at runtime rather than at link time. That is how optional frameworks, plugin architectures and A/B-tested SDKs are loaded, and it is entirely normal, so this ships as INFO inventory rather than a weakness. It matters only as context: an app that also carries obfuscation (SURV-04) or a data broker (TRK-02) can assemble behaviour a static scan cannot see, and dynamic code loading is the mechanism that makes that possible. Note the limit of the signal: an import proves the symbol is linked, not that it is ever called, and iOS forbids loading code that is not already in the signed bundle. (MASWE-0049)
findings.title: Dynamic loader in use (dlopen / dlsym)
findings.why: dlopen/dlsym are present in the binary.

findings.title: Associated domains / universal links

findings.explanation: The app declares com.apple.developer.devicecheck.appattest-environment, so it uses App Attest to prove to its own server that requests come from a genuine, unmodified build. This is a hardening measure, reported as inventory. The entitlement's value (development vs production) is not visible from the key alone; a development environment shipped to the App Store would be a real defect, and needs a value-level check to catch.
findings.title: App Attest / DeviceCheck attestation in use (positive signal)
findings.why: A positive signal: the app attests itself to its backend.

findings.explanation: Third-party code from Google (US) is embedded via 2 SDK(s): Firebase Analytics, Google Ads. Each embedded SDK is a supply-chain dependency that can collect data and update its own behaviour.
findings.remediation: Inventory embedded SDKs and their data collection; remove unused SDKs and pin/verify their distribution to reduce supply-chain exposure.
findings.title: Embedded SDK provenance: Google
findings.why: An inventory of who owns the embedded SDKs. Ownership is not a weakness; data-broker and AI recipients carry their own findings under TRK-02 and TRK-05.

findings.explanation: Info.plist records MinimumOSVersion 15.6, the iOS 26.5 SDK (iphoneos26.5) and Xcode 26.6. The minimum decides which platform protections the app can count on; the SDK decides which current platform behaviour it opts into.

findings.explanation: Imports the C function getifaddrs() which lists every network interface. NOTE: getifaddrs is also the standard primitive for plain reachability and local-IP discovery and is linked by many networking SDKs, so the import alone is a weak VPN signal that fires on most apps. MASTG / privacy-guide VPN detection keys on NEVPNManager or an explicit tunnel-interface name (utun/ppp/ipsec), kept here as an informational marker only.
findings.title: Imports getifaddrs() for network interface enumeration
findings.why: Reading network interfaces and proxy settings on the device meets none of the WP248 criteria by itself.

findings.explanation: Calls _dyld_image_count / _dyld_get_image_name, can be used to detect injected dylibs (tweaks, Frida gadget). NOTE: these symbols are also used by crash reporters, analytics SDKs and the Swift runtime to enumerate loaded images, so bare presence is not anti-analysis. OWASP MASTG anti-debugging tests key on ptrace / sysctl(P_TRACED) rather than dyld enumeration, so this is an informational capability marker, not a weakness.
findings.title: dyld image-list introspection

findings.explanation: The bundle references 1 endpoint(s) whose owner is based in US, owners: Apple. The country is the owning organisation's home jurisdiction from the tracker database, not where a server is hosted, and a referenced endpoint is not observed traffic. If the app sends personal data there, it is a third-country transfer: whether that is lawful depends on the safeguards, purpose and paperwork behind it, none of which is visible in a binary. US holds no EU adequacy decision, so a transfer there needs an Art. 46 safeguard or an Art. 49 derogation.

findings.explanation: The main Mach-O is encrypted by the App Store. Static string scanning of its TEXT segment won't work without a decrypted dump (e.g., via frida-ios-dump or bagbak on a jailbroken device). Embedded frameworks and dylibs are USUALLY ENCRYPTED TOO (measured 91% across the reference corpus; in half of apps every Mach-O is encrypted), so TEXT-segment string recall is limited bundle-wide, not just for the main binary. What still survives encryption is __LINKEDIT: symbols, imported/defined symbol names, ObjC selectors and linked dylibs, which is why symbol-based detection carries this scan rather than string matching.
findings.remediation: For full TEXT-segment coverage, supply a decrypted .ipa produced by frida-ios-dump or bagbak from a jailbroken device. Resource files, plists, entitlements, symbols, selectors and linked dylibs are still scanned in the meantime.
findings.title: Main executable is FairPlay-encrypted
findings.why: Scan metadata: what the scanner could and could not see.
